text: The future of news – coming from a fun circle

There is a great historical irony at the heart of the current transformation of news. The industry is being reshaped by technology – but by undermining the mass media's business models, technology is, in many ways, returning the industry to the more vibrant and discursive ways of the European pre-industrial era.

but by undermining the mass media's business models, technology is, in many ways, returning the industry to the more vibrant and discursive ways of the European pre-industrial era.

text: Until the early 19th century, there was no technology for disseminating news to large numbers of people in a short space of time. It travelled as people chatted in marketplaces or exchanged news with their friends. This phenomenon can be traced back to over 2,000 years ago to the time of the Roman Empire, when members of the upper classes kept each other informed with a multitude of letters. In addition, official gazettes known as the acta diurna were displayed in the centre of Rome each day. These were carved on stone or metal and included details of the results of legal proceedings, as well as other information such as the births and deaths of prominent people. Such news travelled along social networks because there was no other channel for it.

text: The introduction of the printing press in Europe in the 15th century greatly increased the speed with which multiple copies of documents could be produced but distribution still relied on personal connections. In early 1518, Martin Luther's writings on religion spread around Germany in two weeks as they were carried from one town to the next. In Britain in 1588, printed sheets of paper which spread information about current affairs in the form of songs covered the defeat of the Spanish Armada, among many other events.

text: However, these documents were unlike newspapers in that they only contained information about a single topic. Newspapers which included a variety of topics started to become common in the 17th century. They had small, local circulations, and were written by ordinary people rather than by journalists. They contained a mix of opinionated editorials, news, gossip and ideas related to particular social circles or communities. Again, they were essentially social media.

text: The invention of the steam press in the early 19th century and the emergence of mass-market newspapers, therefore marked a profound shift. The new technologies of mass dissemination made it possible to reach large numbers of people with unprecedented speed and efficiency, but put control of the flow of information into the hands of a select few. This trend accelerated with the advent of radio and television in the 20th century. In these media organisations, news was gathered by journalists and disseminated to a mass audience along with advertising which helped to finance the whole operation.

text: Since the end of the 20th century, the internet has disrupted this model and enabled the social aspect of media to reassert itself. In many ways, news is going back to its pre-industrial form, but supercharged by the internet. Cameraphones and social media may seem entirely new, but their use by the public echoes the ways in which people used to collect, share and exchange information in the past. Internet entrepreneur Craig Newmark compares people like Martin Luther to modern bloggers, claiming that in coming years the media and political landscapes will be very different, being controlled not only by influential people but also to an increasing degree by social networks in different forms.

text: News is also becoming more diverse as publishing tools become widely available, barriers to entry fall, and new models become possible. At the same time it is becoming more opinionated and biased rather as it was in the 16th and 17th centuries.

text: Not surprisingly, the conventional news organisations that grew up in the past 170 years are having a lot of trouble adjusting. The mass media era now looks like an exceptional and relatively brief period that is now coming to an end. 'But it was long enough for several generations of journalists to grow up within it, so the laws of the mass media came to be seen as the laws of media in general,' says Jay Rosen, professor of journalism at New York University. 'And when you've built your whole career on that, it isn't easy to say, well, actually, that was just a phase. That's why a lot of us think that it's only going to be generational change that's going to solve this problem.' A new generation that has grown up with digital tools is already devising extraordinary new things to do with them, rather than simply using them to preserve the old models. Some existing media organisations will survive the transition; many will not.

text: The biggest shift is that ordinary people are playing a more active role in journalism, along with a host of technology firms, news start-ups and not-for-profit groups. Social media are certainly not a temporary obsession, and their impact is only just beginning to be felt. Successful media organisations will be the ones that accept this new reality. They need to reorient themselves towards serving readers rather than advertisers, embrace social features and collaboration, and stop trying to erect barriers around journalism to protect their position. The digital future of news has much in common with its chaotic ink-stained past.
